title: Transthoracic echocardiography uses to diagnose proximal aortic dissections in the emergency department: A systematic review
description: Acute type A aortic dissection is among the most dangerous cardiovascular emergencies. Our goals were to gather the most up-to-date clinical data on TTE's diagnostic test accuracy and assess its potential application in the treatment of individuals with probable AD. This study followed the PRISMA guideline. Studies that employed TTE to examine type A or ascending dissection in people, whether randomized or non-randomized, were included because they met a clear reference standard. We searched, Embase, Scopus, MEDLINE, and Web of Science, the search was conducted without regard to language and includes studies published between 2014 and 2024. We found that patients with suspected type A AD can be triaged quickly using TTE as a first-line method. It provides emergency physicians with vital information to assist them make decisions about whether to transfer patients to specialized institutions or proceed swiftly to advanced aortic imaging procedures. TTE cannot be used as a stand-alone test to rule in and rule out type A AD, even when it is used in conjunction with the AD risk score classification. Preliminary findings indicate that TTE can rapidly provide critical diagnostic information in patients presenting with shock or hypotension, but more thorough investigation is required.

title: Diagnosis of acute myocardial ischemia in patients presenting with chest pain in the emergency department using clinical measures and cardiac ultrasonography: A systematic review
description: Background: Chest pain is a common cause of emergency department (ED) visits and presents a diagnostic challenge due to its wide range of etiologies. Traditional diagnostic methods, such as electrocardiography (ECG) and cardiac biomarkers, insufficient in early or atypical presentations. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) emerged as adjuncts for rapid bedside assessment. Our study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of POCUS and TTE in acute myocardial ischemia in patients presenting with chest pain, dyspnea, or suspected acute coronary syndromes (ACS) in the ED. Methods: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Studies included if assessed adult ED patients using POCUS or TTE for chest pain or cardiopulmonary symptoms. Data extracted on study design, demographics, inclusion criteria, ultrasound protocol, operator type, target conditions, reference standards, and diagnostic outcomes. Seven studies involving 2,727 patients were included. Results: POCUS and TTE improved diagnostic accuracy, increased physicians’ confidence, and reduced time to diagnosis. Sensitivity ranged from 60% to 92%, and specificity from 26% to 99%. The SEARCH 8Es and A–F mnemonic protocols were effective in rapid ED settings. POCUS shows better performance than chest X-ray in identifying pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion. Conclusion: POCUS and TTE are good diagnostic tools in the ED setting for patients with suspected myocardial ischemia. These imaging modalities can enhance diagnostic precision and expedite appropriate management when integrated with clinical and laboratory assessments.

title: Multimodal AI-Augmented Radiomics and Spectral Doppler Ultrasound for Early Prediction of Pre-Eclampsia
description: Abstract Pre-eclampsia remains a major cause of global maternal morbidity and mortality. Existing predictive models have limitations in sensitivity, specificity, and biomarker standardization. This study evaluates AI-driven ultrasound biomarkers that integrate self-supervised deep learning (SSDL), hybrid graph neural networks (HGNNs), and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to enhance early risk prediction. The goal is to improve stratification using placental texture analysis, hemodynamic modeling, and maternal serum biomarkers. A systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA guidelines will synthesize data from PubMed, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible studies must assess AI-enhanced ultrasound biomarkers for pre-eclampsia prediction. AI models incorporate federated learning for generalizability and explainability frameworks (SHAP, Grad-CAM, LIME) for transparent clinical interpretation. Comparative analyses are conducted against traditional classifiers, and a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis estimates pooled diagnostic accuracy metrics. Preliminary findings suggest that AI-enhanced radiomics and spectral Doppler biomarkers achieve AUC-ROC values between 0.90–0.97, outperforming conventional methods. Multi-center analyses show statistical superiority ( p < 0.001) over standard screening approaches, confirming cross-populational reproducibility. These findings demonstrate that AI-enhanced placental imaging and hemodynamic modeling enable earlier risk stratification, improved decision-making, and reduced diagnostic uncertainty. Conclusions This study supports AI-augmented radiomics and spectral Doppler ultrasound as a scalable, interpretable, and globally adaptable framework for pre-eclampsia prediction. The combination of Bayesian probabilistic modeling and radiomics-based profiling addresses traditional sonographic limitations while explainability frameworks enhance physician trust in AI-assisted maternal–fetal diagnostics. title: Comparative Diagnostic and Prognostic Utility of Non-Invasive MR, 4D-Flow CMR, CT, and Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in Pulmonary Hypertension: A Systematic Review
description: Background: Accurate prognostication and risk stratification in pulmonary hypertension (PH), particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), remain critical yet challenging. With the evolution of noninvasive imaging, modalities such as echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), 4D-flow CMR, and computed tomography (CT) have shown promise in assessing right ventricular (RV) structure and function and predicting clinical outcomes. Purpose: This systematic review aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and prognostic value of advanced non-invasive imaging techniques in sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and mortality outcomes. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, seven high-quality studies published between 2021 and 2025 were included. These studies employed imaging modalities across diverse international populations. QUADAS-2 was used to assess risk of bias. Outcomes of interest were sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and mortality. Results: CMR and 4D-flow CMR showed superior diagnostic accuracy (AUC up to 0.91) and strong associations with RV end-systolic volume, VO₂, and ventilatory efficiency. CT-derived RV/LV ratios and echocardiographic strain markers emerged as independent predictors of MACE (Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events) and mortality. Consistency in follow-up timing and methodological rigor across studies strengthened the reliability of findings. Conclusion: Advanced imaging biomarkers from echocardiography, CMR, and CT demonstrate significant prognostic utility in PH. Integration of these modalities into clinical pathways could enhance early diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring. Standardization of imaging protocols remains a necessary next step for global application.

title: Optimization of the Diagnostic Algorithm in Appendicitis: The Role of Clinical Scores (Alvarado, AIR Score)
description: Introduction: Acute appendicitis remains a leading cause of emergency abdominal surgery. Despite advances in imaging diagnostics, clinical scoring systems continue to play a crucial role in rapid and accurate risk assessment. The most widely used are the Alvarado score and the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) score. Materials and Methods: A retrospective single-center study was conducted on 124 patients operated for acute appendicitis at the Department of Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic Surgery, University Hospital “Alexandrovska,” between 2018 and 2025. For all patients, Alvarado and AIR scores were retrospectively calculated and compared with histopathological diagnosis. Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values were determined for various cutoff thresholds. Results: An Alvarado score ≥7 demonstrated 82% sensitivity and 68% specificity, whereas an AIR score ≥5 achieved 88% sensitivity and 74% specificity. When combined with C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, overall diagnostic accuracy increased to 90%. Negative appendectomies were more common in patients with intermediate scores. Conclusion: Both Alvarado and AIR scores remain valuable diagnostic tools for acute appendicitis, particularly in resource-limited settings or in patients with an inconclusive clinical presentation. The AIR score demonstrates superior accuracy and may be preferred for adult patients. Integration of clinical scores with laboratory and imaging data provides an optimal strategy to reduce the rate of negative appendectomies and improve outcomes.

title: Atypical clinical presentation of acute appendicitis: diagnostic challenges
description: Acute appendicitis remains one of the most common causes of surgical emergencies. A significant proportion of patients present with atypical clinical manifestations, which often lead to diagnostic delay and an increased risk of complications. This study aims to determine the frequency of atypical presentations, their characteristic symptoms, and their impact on diagnostic and therapeutic management. Materials and Methods: A retrospective study was conducted on 124 patients who underwent surgery for acute appendicitis at the Department of General and Hepato-Pancreatic Surgery, University Hospital “Alexandrovska,” between 2018 and 2025.Of 124 patients, 38 were men (30.6%) and 86 women (69.4%), with a mean age of 37.7 years.  Results: Atypical clinical presentation was observed in 34 patients (27.4%). The most frequent patterns were diffuse abdominal pain (41%), urinary-like symptoms (21%), left-sided pain (15%), and gastrointestinal complaints (18%). The mean diagnostic delay in the atypical group was 19 hours, compared with 7 hours in the typical group (p < 0.05). Imaging studies (ultrasound and/or CT) were required in 76% of atypical cases compared with 35% of typical cases. Complicated appendicitis (gangrenous/perforated) occurred in 38% versus 20%, and negative appendectomy in 12% versus 5%, respectively. Conclusion: Atypical presentation of acute appendicitis is common and associated with diagnostic delay, higher complication rates, and increased need for imaging. Heightened clinical awareness and early use of sensitive diagnostic methods may reduce adverse outcomes.

title: Socio-psychological aspects of the military aggression in Ukraine: a focal point on women's reproductive health
description: The review article analyzes national and foreign scientific researches on the impact of social and-psychological aspects of the military aggression in Ukraine on women’s reproductive health. The relevance of this problem has been studied since the beginning of the aggression in eastern Ukraine and Crimea, when a completely new segment of the population first appeared – internally displaced persons (IDPs). The full-scale invasion in Ukraine, which has been ongoing since February 2022, continues to destroy the lives of civilians and infrastructure, leading to large-scale internal migration and forced departure of the population outside the country. The criticality of the humanitarian catastrophe is confirmed by the fact that by the beginning of 2025, 12.7 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance, and the military aggression has become the largest one in Europe. According to various sources, from 8 to 10 million Ukrainians were forced to leave their homes, including 3.7 million who became IDPs, most of whom are women and children. The analysis of foreign and Ukrainian scientific publications shows that the consequences of traumatic events during war are symptoms of anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, which are caused by changes in habitual living conditions, permanent uncertainty, threats to personal safety and the safety of immediate family, loss of loved ones, etc. The data presented confirm that pregnant women are most susceptible to traumatic events and their consequences during hostilities, on whom the war factor can have a critical impact, increasing the risk of adverse obstetric and perinatal consequences. The cessation of the effect of such a significant stress factor on the organism as the military action is impossible before its end, regardless of whether the woman continues to be in her place of permanent residence, has moved to a safer region of the country, or is a refugee who has left the country. This view of the problem confirms the need for a comprehensive approach to diagnosing psychological disorders in pregnant women and requires the immediate need to develop individual programs for medical and psychological support for women during pregnancy.

title: Post-appendectomy stump appendicitis case report
description: Introduction: Appendicitis is a very prevalent pathology and appendectomy is one of the most common procedures worldwide. The exact cause of appendicitis is not fully understood, however multifactorial associations have been associated.  Stump appendicitis is the inflammation of the residual appendix, it is a rare complication, mimicking acute appendicitis and leading to delayed diagnosis and increased morbidity. We present a case of a patient who developed stump appendicitis after an open appendectomy. Case presentation: A 48-year-old male presented with 24-hour right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and distension, complicated by prior emergency left hemicolectomy with appendectomy for perforated sigmoid colon. Relevant history included left renal agenesis, multiple trauma sequelae and substance use disorder in remission. Examination revealed right lower quadrant tenderness, leucocytosis with neutrophilia, and elevated CRP -  a typical clinic for appendicitis. CT confirmed a 20×22 mm inflamed appendiceal stump, subsequently resected via open surgery.  Conclusion: Stump appendicitis, though rare, necessitates consideration in patients with right lower quadrant pain, even post-appendectomy. Prompt diagnosis and resection are optimizing outcomes.

title: Validity of screening instruments for the detection of dementia and mild cognitive impairment in hospital inpatients: A systematic review of diagnostic accuracy studies
description: Introduction As the population ages, Alzheimer's disease and other subtypes of dementia are becoming increasingly prevalent. However, in recent years, diagnosis has often been delayed or not made at all. Thus, improving the rate of diagnosis has become an integral part of national dementia strategies. Although screening for dementia remains controversial, the case is strong for screening for dementia and other forms of cognitive impairment in hospital inpatients. For this reason, the objective of this systematic review was to provide clinicians, who wish to implement screening, an up-to-date choice of cognitive tests with the most extensive evidence base for the use in elective hospital inpatients. Methods For this systematic review, PubMed, PsycINFO and Cochrane Library were searched by using a multi-concept search strategy. The databases were accessed on April 10, 2019. All cross-sectional studies that utilized brief, multi-domain cognitive tests as index test and a reference standard diagnosis of dementia or mild cognitive impairment as comparator were included. Only studies conducted in the hospital setting, sampling from unselected, elective inpatients older than 64 were considered. Results Six studies met the inclusion criteria, with a total of 2112 participants. Diagnostic accuracy data for the Six-Item Cognitive Impairment Test, Cognitive Performance Scale, Clock-Drawing Test, Mini-Mental Status Examination, and Time & Change test were extracted and descriptively analyzed. Clinical and methodological heterogeneity between the studies precluded performing a meta-analysis. Discussion This review found only a small number of instruments and was not able to recommend a single best instrument for use in a hospital setting. Although it was not possible to estimate the pooled operating characteristics, the included description of instrument characteristics, the descriptive analysis of performance measures, and the critical evaluation of the reporting studies may contribute to clinician's choice of the screening instrument that fits best their purpose.

title: ECG CRITERIA FOR LEFT ATRIAL ENLARGEMENT VS. ECHO-MEASURED LA VOLUME AND STRAIN: DIAGNOSTIC THRESHOLDS AND CLINICAL UTILITY, A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
description: Abstract Background: Left atrial (LA) size and function are routinely quantified by echocardiography using left atrial volume index (LAVI) and speckle-tracking LA strain. Electrocardiographic (ECG) criteria, such as P-wave duration, notching (“P-mitrale”), and P-wave terminal force in V1 (PTFV1), are widely used as low-cost surrogates, yet their agreement with echo-defined enlargement or dysfunction remains debated. Objective: To synthesize evidence comparing ECG criteria of “left atrial enlargement (LAE)” against echo-measured LA volume and/or LA strain, and to appraise diagnostic thresholds and clinical utility. Methods: Following PRISMA guidance, we searched major databases to October 19, 2025. We included original studies in adults that directly compared ECG indices with transthoracic echo reference standards (2D/3D LAVI and/or LA strain). Twelve studies met inclusion for the results synthesis; 10 additional papers informed background and interpretation. Results: Across heterogeneous cohorts, traditional ECG LAE criteria showed modest sensitivity and variable specificity for detecting increased LAVI. PTFV1 and P-wave peak time correlated most consistently with LAVI, while LA strain (reservoir) related inversely to P-wave indices and PTFV1. Proposed ECG cutoffs differed by population (hemodialysis vs. hypertension vs. valvular disease). Conclusions: ECG abnormalities reflect atrial electrical remodeling but incompletely capture echo-defined atrial dilation or dysfunction. Multiparametric ECG assessment may aid triage, yet LAVI and LA strain remain the reference for diagnosis and risk stratification.

title: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF MODIFIED GRAM STAIN TECHNIQUES FOR THE DETECTION AND INTERPRETATION OF MYCOBACTERIUM SPP
description: This systematic review examines the diagnostic interpretation of Gram stain and modified staining techniques for Mycobacterium species, focusing on improvements introduced by auramine fluorescence, LED microscopy, and automation. Mycobacterium spp. possess lipid-rich cell walls that resist conventional Gram staining, often producing inconsistent results that hinder accurate detection. Over the past decade, advances in staining chemistry and image-assisted microscopy have sought to enhance diagnostic accuracy and laboratory efficiency. This review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, analyzing peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2025 from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Findings indicate that auramine-based LED fluorescence microscopy demonstrates higher sensitivity and throughput compared to Ziehl–Neelsen and traditional Gram staining, while machine-assisted auramine interpretation further improves reliability. Although modified Gram protocols show potential for differentiating acid-fast organisms, results remain variable. The review underscores the continued importance of fluorescence microscopy as the standard for mycobacterial detection and highlights the need for further research on standardized protocols and automated interpretation systems.

title: Association between intelectin-1, sleep quality, and insulin resistance in infertile women of reproductive age
description: Intelectin-1, in addition to its anti-inflammatory activity, may play a role in the pathogenesis of type II diabetes and sleep disorders. However, its exact role in humans still requires further investigation. This study was conducted on 175 women, divided into two groups: 90 patients with infertility (cases) and 85 fertile women (controls). In addition to sociodemographic and anthropometric measurements, the study collected information on intelectin-1, the Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI), fasting blood sugar, insulin level, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), the quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI), the homeostatic model assessment for β-cell function (HOMA-β), insulin sensitivity, and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH). Intelectin-1 was shown to be a reliable biomarker for the assessment of menstrual irregularity and sleep quality. Moreover, intelectin-1 showed a significant negative correlation with body mass index, menstrual regularity, PSQI, and fasting blood sugar regulation, while it had a significant positive correlation with HOMA-β and AMH.

title: ЦИТОХИМИЯ НОРМАЛЬНЫХ И ЛЕЙКЕМИЧЕСКИХ ЛИМФОЦИТОВ
description: Цитохимия остаётся важным дополнением к морфологическому и иммунологическому исследованию лимфоцитов при диагностике гематологических заболеваний. В обзоре рассмотрены цитохимические особенности нормальных лимфоцитов и их изменений при различных формах лимфоидных лейкозов (острый лимфобластный лейкоз — ОЛЛ, хронический лимфоцитарный лейкоз — ХЛЛ и др.), методики окраски (MPO, Sudan Black B, PAS, не-специфическая эстераза, кислая фосфатаза и др.), диагностическая ценность цитохимии в современной лабораторной практике и её соотношение с иммуннофенотипированием и молекулярной диагностикой. Обобщены данные последних публикаций (2020–2025 гг.) о чувствительности и специфичности отдельных цитохимических реакций, роли цитохимии в ресурс-ограниченных условиях и её месте в комбинированном алгоритме диагностики лейкемий. Представлены рекомендации по использованию цитохимии как дополнения к морфологии и иммунофенотипированию.

title: Possibilities of digital breast tomosynthesis and full-field digital mammography in the visualization of breast calcifications
description: Calcifications are the common findings which are visualized on full-field digital mammography (FFDM) in about 80% of cases. Most calcifications are benign changes that do not pose any threat to the lives of patients. However, suspicious calcifications can also be detected in the breast, which, when are verified, can lead to the discovery of malignant changes in one-third of cases. In recent years, the number of uses of digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) has been increasing due to the greater sensitivity and specificity of the method compared to FFDM. The objective: to evaluate the impact of DBT on improvement of the imaging of breast calcifications on FFDM. Materials and methods. We have analyzed FFDM, DBT, and ultrasound (US) test results of 101 women 31–85 years old with and without breast calcifications. Results. The study found that the sensitivity of DBT was 95.2% (p < 0.05), FFDM – 98.8% (p < 0.05), and 21.7% – for breast US examination. The specificity for DBT was 83.3%, while for FFDM – 94.4% (p < 0.05). At the same time, there was no statistically significant difference in the diagnosis of breast calcifications between DBT and FFDM. However, there was a statistically significant advantage of DBT and FFDM over US imaging of breast calcifications (p < 0.01). Conclusions. DBT does not have a significant impact on the imaging of calcifications compared to FFDM, but both methods are significantly superior in sensitivity and specificity to US examination in the imaging of breast calcifications.

title: Digital Transformation and Innovation in Contemporary Nursing: Challenges and Opportunities
description: Digital Transformation and Innovation in Contemporary Nursing: Challenges and Opportunities By Jocarla Nicolina Cavalcante Abstract Contemporary nursing is undergoing a period of transition marked by the growing incorporation of digital technologies and innovative methodologies in healthcare services. This study aims to analyze, in light of scientific literature, the impacts of digital transformation on nursing practice, considering benefits, ethical challenges, and implications for professional training. National and international articles on telemedicine, artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and electronic health records were reviewed. The results indicate that adopting digital technologies can enhance efficiency, care personalization, and patient safety but also demands new skills from professionals and raises ethical dilemmas related to privacy and humanization of care. It is concluded that a balanced integration between technological innovation and patient-centered care constitutes the path toward strengthening nursing in the 21st century. Keywords: Nursing; Digital transformation; Innovation; Health technology; Humanization. Introduction Technological advancement in recent decades has led to profound changes in healthcare services, presenting both challenges and new possibilities for professional practice. The so-called digital transformation—characterized by the incorporation of tools such as telemedicine, artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and integrated information systems—is reshaping care and management processes in hospitals, clinics, and community services (TOPAZ & BOWLES, 2016). In nursing, these transformations directly affect how work is organized, patients are monitored, interventions are planned, and teams are managed. While digital technologies improve efficiency and diagnostic accuracy, they also raise questions about preserving the humanistic dimension of care—the central axis of the profession’s identity (COFEN, 2021). Additionally, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the global adoption of digital solutions. The use of teleconsultations, digital tracking protocols, and remote patient monitoring illustrates how quickly technology became integrated into nursing practice (WHO, 2021). This scenario makes it urgent to debate how to reconcile innovation and humanization, ensuring that digital practice does not depersonalize care. The objective of this article is to discuss the main challenges and opportunities of digital transformation and innovation in contemporary nursing, exploring both its positive impacts on service safety and efficiency and its ethical and social implications. Literature Review Telemedicine and Expanding Access Telemedicine has become one of the main digital tools applied to 21st-century healthcare. Its expansion was driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, which required rapid adaptation of health systems to maintain care despite mobility restrictions. In Brazil, the Ministry of Health’s Emergency Ordinance No. 467/2020 authorized telemedicine on an exceptional basis, allowing nurses to participate in telecare, remote patient follow-up, and chronic condition monitoring (BRASIL, 2020). Tele-nursing has shown great potential in expanding access, especially in geographically isolated regions or those with a shortage of health professionals. Studies suggest that remote nursing consultations can improve treatment adherence, reduce preventable hospitalizations, and promote greater patient engagement in self-care (GOMES et al., 2021). These findings reinforce the need for technological training among nurses and public policies that ensure the continuity of digital care beyond emergency contexts. Artificial Intelligence and Big Data The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data analytics has significantly transformed healthcare practice, directly impacting nursing. Machine learning algorithms are already applied in intensive care units for risk stratification, early detection of clinical deterioration, and complication prediction (TOPAZ & BOWLES, 2016). These advances offer crucial support for nurses’ decision-making processes, providing predictive tools for care prioritization and resource allocation. However, AI use requires new competencies from nurses, including digital literacy, critical thinking regarding automated results, and ethical evaluation of data usage. Literature emphasizes that blind trust in intelligent systems can create risks, highlighting the importance of human clinical judgment as an indispensable complement to technology (CUMMINGS et al., 2018). Robotics and Hospital Automation Robotics is another emerging field in healthcare, increasingly present in hospital environments. Robots are used in logistics tasks such as transporting medications and supplies, disinfecting environments, and even assisting in basic care activities like patient mobility support. Research indicates that when properly integrated, these technologies can free nurses from repetitive tasks, allowing them to focus on complex and human-centered activities (MISKELLY & DUNCAN, 2014). Nonetheless, this introduction raises ethical and labor concerns. The potential partial replacement of the workforce and high implementation costs generate debate. For nursing, the challenge is to balance robots as allies in care while preserving the profession’s fundamentally human essence. Electronic Health Records and Information Systems The electronic health record (EHR) is one of the most widespread digital tools in healthcare institutions, transforming how clinical information is recorded, accessed, and shared. Its use enables greater traceability, data integration across sectors, and longitudinal patient monitoring. Despite its advantages, literature points to key limitations: system interoperability failures, increased workload due to non-intuitive interfaces, and privacy and security risks (VENTER et al., 2018). In this context, nurses play a crucial role as both managers of clinical information and active agents in developing safe practices for data recording and sharing. Ethical Dimension and Humanization While promising, digital transformation in healthcare raises serious ethical challenges. Issues such as data privacy and confidentiality, unequal access to technologies, digital exclusion of vulnerable populations, and informed consent in digital platforms are widely discussed in the literature (SHAPIRO & STEFKOVICH, 2016). Thus, nursing leadership is critical to ensuring that technological innovation is implemented equitably, transparently, and inclusively. Nurse leaders must act as mediators between innovation and humanization, ensuring that technology serves as a support tool rather than a factor of care depersonalization. Methodology This study is characterized as a narrative literature review conducted between May and August 2023. The databases Scielo, PubMed, Lilacs, and Google Scholar were consulted, prioritizing national and international scientific publications from 2010 to 2023. Keywords included “nursing and digital technology,” “telemedicine and nursing,” “artificial intelligence in healthcare,” “hospital robotics,” and “electronic health record.” Included materials comprised original articles, systematic reviews, institutional reports from the World Health Organization, and Brazilian regulatory documents such as ordinances and resolutions from the Ministry of Health and the Federal Nursing Council (COFEN). The narrative review method was chosen for its flexibility in integrating diverse perspectives and synthesizing heterogeneous results, enabling critical and contextual analysis of the challenges and opportunities in digital transformation in nursing. Although it does not follow the strict protocols of systematic reviews, this approach is suitable for promoting reflection and theoretical construction in rapidly evolving fields such as digital health. Conclusion Digital transformation in nursing represents an irreversible process driven by the demands of an increasingly complex, globalized, and data-oriented healthcare system. Tools such as telemedicine, artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and electronic health records provide tangible benefits in efficiency, safety, and personalized care—positioning nursing as a key player in integrating technology and healthcare. However, these advances are not without challenges. Ethics, privacy, data protection, and maintaining patient-centered care require constant attention to prevent innovation from leading to dehumanization or digital exclusion. The central question for contemporary nursing is not whether to adopt new technologies, but how to do so responsibly, equitably, and with human values at the core. Thus, the future of nursing will depend on the profession’s ability to harmoniously integrate technological innovation and humanization. This requires developing leaders capable of balancing organizational efficiency with ethical principles, fostering inclusive environments, and promoting evidence-based interdisciplinary practices. Investing in digital competencies for nurses—alongside strengthening inclusive public policies and robust regulatory frameworks—will be essential for ensuring that technology becomes a strategic ally rather than a threat to the profession’s essence. In doing so, nursing will continue to transform technological challenges into opportunities for innovation, always preserving care as the nucleus of its identity. References BRASIL. title: The Secure Future of Medical AI on Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning-A Systematic Review
description: The study presents a comprehensive review of Federated Learning , outlining a practical method for building strong Artificial Intelligence models in the healthcare industry while maintaining patient privacy.A key issue identified is that privacy laws like GDPR and HIPAA often result in medical data being scattered across different organizations, complicating the development of dependable and broadly applicable AI solutions. FL addresses this by allowing teams to train models together without sharing the actual sensitive data. Research underscores that traditional Federated Learning faces challenges due to non-IID data distributions and susceptibility to privacy inference attacks.This paper examine advanced frameworks that implement a multi-layered defense system apply techniques like Secure Multi-Party Computation, Homomorphic Encryption, and Differential Privacy to tackle these issues. The key advancements discussed affect hierarchical architectures with edge servers to enhance efficiency, dynamic aggregation strategies to manage data heterogeneity, and adaptive privacy budget allocation to achieve an optimal balance between privacy and utility. The conceptual framework of this study highlights how these enhanced federated learning approaches offer robust privacy safeguards and achieve remarkable diagnostic accuracy, often matching or even exceptional traditional centralized models. However, despite these achievements, the main challenge—especially when using advanced encryption techniques—remains the substantial processing overhead.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Histopathology versus Microbiological Methods in Fungal Infections: A Systematic Review of H&E, PAS, and GMS Staining Compared with Culture and PCR
description: Background : Fungal infections are an increasing cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly among immunocompromised patients. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for timely initiation of antifungal therapy. While histopathology using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS), and Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) stains remains the mainstay of rapid diagnosis, its diagnostic accuracy compared with microbiological techniques such as culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) remains variable. Objective : To systematically evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy of histopathological staining methods (H&E, PAS, GMS) with culture and PCR in the diagnosis of fungal infections across clinical specimens. Methods : A systematic literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar was performed for studies published between January 2000 and August 2025. Studies comparing histopathological and microbiological methods with reported sensitivity and specificity were included. Data were pooled using a random-effects model, and study quality was assessed using QUADAS-2 guidelines. Results : A total of 26 studies involving 3,428 clinical specimens met inclusion criteria. Pooled sensitivity and specificity for H&E were 68% and 82%, for PAS 82% and 88%, and for GMS 89% and 91%, respectively. Fungal culture demonstrated high specificity (97%) but low sensitivity (58%), while PCR showed superior accuracy with pooled sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 95%. Combining histopathology (PAS or GMS) with PCR yielded the highest diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity 96%, specificity 94%). Subgroup analysis revealed that GMS and PCR performed best for Aspergillus and Mucorales, while PAS showed better sensitivity for Candida and Histoplasma infections. Conclusion : Histopathology remains a rapid, cost-effective, and essential method for early detection of fungal infections, particularly when culture results are delayed or negative. GMS and PAS provide superior morphological detail, while PCR offers enhanced sensitivity and species-level identification. A combined diagnostic approach integrating histopathology with molecular methods yields the highest diagnostic accuracy and should be considered the optimal strategy for managing suspected fungal infections.

title: Evaluation of H&E, PAS, and GMS Stains Compared with Culture and PCR in Fungal Infection Diagnosis: A Systematic Review
description: Background : Fungal infections are increasingly recognized as major causes of morbidity and mortality, especially among immunocompromised patients. Timely and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective management. Histopathological stains such as Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS), and Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) are widely used for tissue-based fungal detection, yet their diagnostic accuracy compared with culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) remains variable. Aim : To systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of H&E, PAS, and GMS stains in detecting fungal infections, and to compare their efficacy with culture and PCR as reference standards. Methods : A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases was conducted for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Eligible studies compared one or more histopathological stains with culture and/or PCR in human tissue specimens. Data on sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic concordance were extracted and analyzed qualitatively following PRISMA guidelines. Results : Twenty-seven studies (n = 2,345 samples) met inclusion criteria. GMS demonstrated the highest sensitivity (80–98%) for fungal detection, followed by PAS (70–90%) and H&E (50–80%). Specificity across stains was consistently above 85%. Culture showed variable sensitivity (40–70%) and longer turnaround time, while PCR achieved superior accuracy (sensitivity >95%, specificity >98%) even in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues. Combining histopathology with PCR improved diagnostic yield to over 98%. Conclusion : While GMS remains the most reliable histopathological stain for detecting fungal elements, PCR provides the highest diagnostic precision and species-level identification. Integration of histopathology, culture, and molecular methods ensures optimal accuracy and rapid diagnosis of fungal infections, particularly in critically ill or immunocompromised patients Fungal infection, Histopathology, H&E, PAS, GMS, Culture, PCR, Diagnostic accuracy.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Paediatric Pyogenic Meningitis: Correlation Between CSF Cytology, Culture, and Molecular Findings
description: Background:  Paediatric pyogenic meningitis remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality despite advances in antimicrobial therapy and vaccination. Rapid and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective management. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis forms the cornerstone of diagnosis, but discrepancies between cytological, culture, and molecular findings often complicate clinical interpretation. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and correlation between CSF cytology, bacterial culture, and molecular assays in paediatric pyogenic meningitis. Methods:  A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2000 and September 2025. Studies including paediatric patients (<18 years) with suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis and reporting CSF cytology, culture, and molecular findings were included. Data were extracted and analyzed using RevMan 5.4 and STATA 17. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratios (DOR) were calculated using a random-effects model. Correlation between diagnostic modalities was assessed using Pearson’s correlation coefficient ( r ). Study quality was evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. Results:  Forty-two studies encompassing 8,715 paediatric cases were included. Pooled sensitivity was highest for molecular assays (91.3%; 95% CI: 88.1-94.0), followed by culture (68.5%; 95% CI: 62.4-73.9) and cytology (56.8%; 95% CI: 50.3-62.9). Specificity was highest for culture (95.7%) and combined cytology-culture (95.7%). Incorporation of molecular testing increased overall diagnostic yield by 28.4% in culture-negative cases. A strong positive correlation was found between CSF neutrophilic cytology and molecular positivity ( r  = 0.72,  p  < 0.001). The predominant pathogens identified were  Streptococcus pneumoniae  (42%),  Neisseria meningitidis  (23%), and  Haemophilus influenzae  type b (18%). Heterogeneity among studies was moderate (I² = 62%), with minimal publication bias. Conclusion:  Molecular diagnostic assays markedly improve sensitivity and overall diagnostic accuracy in paediatric pyogenic meningitis, particularly in culture-negative or partially treated cases. Nonetheless, cytology and culture remain essential components of the diagnostic framework, providing rapid inflammatory assessment and antimicrobial guidance. Integration of cytology, culture, and molecular findings offers the most comprehensive and reliable diagnostic approach for paediatric bacterial meningitis, enabling timely and evidence-based therapeutic interventions.

title: AI-POWERED METABOLIC INTELLIGENCE: REDEFINING PERSONALIZED CANCER THERAPY THROUGH MULTI-OMICS DATA
description: Cancer is a worldwide health concern characterised by the unchecked growth, division, and metabolism of tissues and individual cells, which feeds the tumour and permits its proliferation as it becomes resistant to treatment. Since cancer cells can withstand stress and many tumours are diverse, surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation have not shown to be viable long-term remedies. Through the use of glucose, tumour metabolism regulates several cellular metabolisms and is linked to the advancement of cancer. Due to the tumour's incredibly high energy requirements and rapid development, pathways involved in glycolysis, amino acid metabolism, and lipid metabolism are reorganised. These metabolic changes may lead to novel strategies for cancer patients' focused treatments. Therefore, this knowledge of these metabolic alterations will help create more effective and individualised treatment plans. Artificial intelligence has emerged as a greatly improved tool in the field of cancer to help researchers analyse large datasets of genetic and metabolic data to find patterns that would not otherwise be seen. These prediction tools are helpful when dealing with medication resistance, mapping the metabolism of tumours, and finding biomarkers that show how a tumour reacts to particular therapies. The machine learning models use proteomics, genomes, and metabolomics data to improve understanding of tumour behaviour. This makes it possible to develop therapeutic strategies that will stop particular metabolic pathways that are only utilised by malignant cells. AI is also enhancing real-time tumour monitoring, which enables physicians to modify treatment plans according to the distinct metabolic profiles of each patient.

title: Pleural Effusion and Empyema
description: Pleural Effusion and Empyema   Author: Shravani Zade , Khushi Bhandari and Rajat Lande Under the  Guidance of Abdiraimov Isakender sir     Abstract   Background: Pleural effusion, the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, is a frequent clinical phenomenon in most specialties. Its complication to empyema, pus, is a critical and potentially lethal condition, most frequently secondary to pneumonia. Understanding the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and staged treatment is mandatory for any clinical practitioner.   Objective: The aim of this article is to provide an extensive, systematic review of pleural effusion and empyema, amalgamating basic pathophysiology with current clinical guidelines in a bid to create a guide for medical students and junior physicians.   Key Insights: The pathway from simple effusion to complicated empyema takes place along a characterised continuum: the exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organising stages. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical suspicion, imaging (especially bedside ultrasound), and pleural fluid analysis using Light’s criteria[1]. Treatment of empyema is built around the fundamentals of early antibiotic treatment and effective drainage, with progression from tube thoracostomy to video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for more advanced cases. Treatment delayed can lead to prolonged hospital stay, pleural fibrosis, and permanent lung dysfunction.   Conclusion: Pleural effusion and empyema demand a systematic, aggressive approach. The most significant determinants of patient outcome are early recognition of a complex parapneumonic effusion and early intervention to achieve source control. A knowledge of this is critical to prevent severe morbidity and mortality from this common thoracic infection.   1. Introduction   The pleural space, a potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura, normally contains a small amount of fluid (5-15 mL) to facilitate lung movement during respiration. Pleural effusion occurs when there is an imbalance between the formation and resorption of this fluid, leading to pathological accumulation. When this fluid becomes infected, it can progress to a parapneumonic effusion, and if the bacteria are not hindered in their growth, it will evolve into an empyema—the collection of pus in the pleural space. Medical students must know this disease spectrum, as it is a common and instructive example of the evolution of a localized infection into a systemic, surgical process.   2. Pathophysiology and Classification   2.1. Pleural Fluid Dynamics   Under normal circumstances, pleural fluid is formed by filtration from the parietal pleural capillaries (systemic circulation) and absorbed by the visceral pleural capillaries (pulmonary circulation) and lymphatics. An effusion develops due to:   · Increased Hydrostatic Pressure (e.g., Congestive Heart Failure). · Decreased Oncotic Pressure (e.g., Nephrotic Syndrome, Cirrhosis). · Increased Capillary Permeability (e.g., Pneumonia, Malignancy). · Impaired Lymphatic Drainage (e.g., Malignancy).   2.2. Transudate vs. Exudate   The first significant task in the evaluation of an effusion is to categorize it, most commonly using Light’s Criteria[1]. It is an exudate if it meets any of the following:   1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein > 0.5 2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH > 0.6 3. Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH   · Transudates are plasma ultrafiltrates due to systemic processes that change Starling forces (e.g., HF, cirrhosis). They tend to be clear and contain minimal cells. · Exudates result from local disease processes (e.g., infection, inflammation, cancer) that directly impact the pleura, rendering it more permeable.   2.3. The Path to Empyema   Empyema most often develops from a parapneumonic effusion. This development occurs in three stages [2]:   1. Exudative Phase (Simple Parapneumonic Effusion): Pleural hyperpermeability leads to sterile, free-flowing fluid. pH is usually >7.30, normal glucose, and low LDH. This phase may resolve with antibiotics alone. 2. Fibropurulent Stage (Complicated Parapneumonic Effusion/Empyema): Bacteria invade the pleural space, and an intense inflammatory response is triggered. Neutrophils infiltrate, fibrin deposition occurs, and loculations(walls) are created, trapping the fluid. The fluid is now turbid, pH <7.20, glucose low (<60 mg/dL), and LDH elevated. This is the stage at which drainage is required. 3. Organizing Stage (Chronic Empyema): Fibroblasts grow into the exudate to form an inelastic “pleural peel” around the lung. The peel prevents re-expansion of the lung, a condition called “trapped lung.”   3. Etiology and Microbiology   The etiology of pleural effusion is long. Some of the common causes of transudates include CHF and hepatic hydrothorax. Some of the common causes of exudates include pneumonia, malignancy, and pulmonary embolism.   In empyema, community-acquired infections are most frequently caused by Streptococcus species (including S. pneumoniae and S. milleri) and Staphylococcus aureus[3]. Anaerobes (e.g., Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) are also common, especially in aspiration pneumonia. Hospital-acquired (nosocomial) empyemas more often involve Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and Gram-negative rods like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella species.   4. Clinical Presentation   · Symptoms: Fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, and dyspnea are present in most patients. Recent pneumonia is typical. In the elderly or immunocompromised, presentation may be subtle with confusion or functional decline only. · Signs: Diminished breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and decreased tactile fremitus over the effusion may be present on physical examination. Egophony (E-to-A changes) may be heard at the upper border of the effusion.   5. Diagnostic Approach   Systematic diagnostic approach is crucial.   1. Imaging:   · Chest X-Ray (CXR): Initial test, with meniscus sign (costophrenicangle blunting). Decubitus views can assess for layering (free-flowing vs. loculated).   · Computed Tomography (CT): Gold standard for exquisite anatomy. Can identify loculations, pleural thickening, and underlying pulmonary pathology [4]. · Bedside Ultrasound (US): Very useful. More sensitive than CXR for small effusions, distinguishes fluid from consolidation, and most importantly, identifies septations and loculations, which guide thoracentesis [5]. 2. Diagnostic Thoracentesis: Mandatory for pleural fluid analysis. Analysis should be performed for:   · Gross Appearance: Clear (transudate), turbid (exudate), bloody (malignancy, PE), or frankly purulent (empyema). · Cell Count and Differential: Neutrophil predominance suggests acute inflammation/infection.   · Biochemistry: pH, glucose, LDH, and protein (for Light’s criteria).   · Microbiology: Gram stain and culture (aerobic and anaerobic).   · Cytology: For suspected malignancy.   6. Management   Management is staged according to the severity of the effusion/empyema.   1. Antibiotic Therapy: Empiric, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics form the mainstay in the management of any parapneumonic effusion or empyema and should cover the suspected pathogens based on the clinical setting (community vs. hospital-acquired) [6]. The treatment is then modified based on culture. 2. Drainage Procedures:   · Therapeutic Thoracentesis: May be sufficient for small free-flowing complicated effusions. · Tube Thoracostomy (Chest Tube): The primary treatment of confirmed empyema. Small-bore (8-14F) pigtail catheters, placed under US or CT guidance, are now preferred to large-bore tubes due to similar efficacy and better patient tolerance [7]. · Intrapleural Fibrinolytic Therapy: For loculated empyemas that do not drain with a chest tube alone, the use of agents like tPA (tissue Plasminogen Activator) combined with DNase (Dornase Alfa) can effectively lyse fibrinous septations and improve drainage dramatically [8]. The MIST-2 trial established the position of this combination as a standard of care for complex pleural infection. 3. Surgical Management: · Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS): The procedure of choice for failures of medical management with antibiotics and chest tube drainage. VATS enhances direct visualization, lysis of loculations, debridement of infected tissue, and drainage of the pleural space [9]. · Open Thoracotomy and Decortication: Employed in the most chronic, severe phases (organizing stage) when there is a thick pleural peel preventing lung expansion. It involves stripping of the visceral peel to free the entrapped lung. · Open Drainage (Rib Resection): In patients with chronic illness who are not candidates for major decortication, a segment of rib can be resected to create a window for long-term open drainage.   7. Complications and Prognosis   Poorly or untreated empyema can lead to:   · Bronchopleural fistula. · Pleural fibrosis and trapped lung. · Empyema necessitans (spontaneous rupture through the chest wall). · Sepsis and death.   Prognosis is otherwise good with early and appropriate treatment. Delayed treatment is the single most significant factor associated with poor outcome, such as prolonged hospital stay and need for surgery [10].   8. Conclusion   For the medical student, the clinical trajectory from pleural effusion to empyema is a master class in applied pathophysiology. It teaches the importance of a systematic diagnostic approach, starting with Light’s criteria and imaging and progressing to a staged management strategy. The take-home message is one of vigilance: early identification of the signs of a complicated parapneumonic effusion and the understanding that empyema is a surgical disease that needs to be drained with urgency. By adding antimicrobial therapy to adequate source control, we can significantly improve outcomes in patients with this fatal thoracic infection.     References 1. Light, R. W., Macgregor, M. title: Serological Assays of Brucellosis in Unvaccinated Sheep and Goat in Indonesia
description: ABSTRACT:  Brucellosis is recognized as one of the most widespread zoonotic diseases and is often overlooked, impacting livestock populations worldwide. Annual routine screenings utilize serological assays, such as the Rose Bengal test (RBT) and the complement fixation test (CFT), to identify the presence of brucellosis. The present study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic and discriminative performance of the CFT, the locally produced RBT antigen from Indonesia, the commercial RBT antigen (Pourquier), and the indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) using sera from Indonesian goats and sheep. A total of 184 serum samples were collected, including 92 from goats and 92 from sheep. The samples were obtained through jugular venipuncture from animals on small-scale goat and sheep farms in Java Island, Indonesia. The results were analyzed to determine true prevalence (TP), accuracy, and cross-tabulation with parallel interpretation to assess the sensitivity and specificity of each test analysis. The TP of brucellosis in small ruminant serum samples using local RBT, Pourquier RBT, CFT, and indirect ELISA was 6.99%, 9.74%, 0%, and 14.78% in goats, and 6.92%, 20.34%, 0%, and 7.81% in sheep, respectively. Moderate Kappa interrater reliability was observed between the local and Pourquier RBTs for both goats (0.537) and sheep (0.440). The combined RBT sensitivity in goats and sheep was 27% and 20%, respectively, while the combined RBT specificity was 92% in goats and 80.5% in sheep. Using more than one diagnostic method is essential for screening and investigating brucellosis in goat and sheep populations. A combination of RBT and indirect ELISA tests is recommended to identify  Brucella reactors among small ruminants in Indonesia.   https://wvj.science-line.com/attachments/article/88/WVJ15(3)710-719,2025.pdf

title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection and Diagnosis of Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches
description: Breast cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality among women globally, highlighting the critical need for early detection and accurate diagnosis. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing both machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches, have demonstrated significant potential in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, reducing human error, and supporting clinical decision-making. This systematic review critically analyzes existing studies that employ AI for breast cancer detection, focusing on methodological approaches, dataset characteristics, model performance, and interpretability. ML-based techniques, including support vector machines, random forests, and gradient boosting, show promising results in structured datasets, particularly where dataset sizes are limited, and interpretability is essential. In contrast, DL approaches, primarily convolutional neural networks and their variants, outperform ML in raw image analysis, multi-modal imaging, and complex feature extraction, achieving higher accuracy and sensitivity. Hybrid models integrating ML and DL, often augmented with radiomics features, offer a balanced framework, combining high predictive performance with improved interpretability. Additionally, explainable AI (XAI) techniques are increasingly applied to DL models, mitigating the “black-box” problem and fostering clinical trust. Despite these advancements, challenges remain, including the need for large, high-quality, multi-institutional datasets, computational resource demands, and generalizability across diverse populations. Low-resource and portable AI solutions offer potential for broader accessibility, though with modest reductions in predictive performance. Overall, AI demonstrates transformative potential in early breast cancer detection, particularly when combined with hybrid and explainable frameworks. Future research should prioritize multi-modal integration, rigorous cross-center validation, and deployment strategies that balance accuracy, interpretability, and accessibility, ultimately facilitating clinical adoption and improving patient outcomes.

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF SALIVARY MICROBIOLOGICAL TESTS FOR PERIODONTITIS AND CARIES: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
description: Abstract Saliva is an attractive diagnostic medium for oral diseases because it is non-invasive, inexpensive, and easy to collect at scale. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of salivary microbiological tests for periodontitis and dental caries. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to 26 October 2025 for original studies that measured salivary microorganisms against accepted clinical reference standards for periodontitis or caries. Twelve original studies met inclusion criteria (periodontitis, n=6, caries, n=6). For periodontitis, multiplex qPCR panels and 16S-based models showed good to excellent discrimination: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) commonly ≥0.90 for multifeature indices, with sensitivity,specificity typically >80% in internal validation. Single-species cut-offs performed inconsistently. For caries, very high salivary Streptococcus mutans by culture predicted longitudinal caries progression in preschoolers, and several 16S, qPCR models discriminated severe early childhood caries with moderate-to-good accuracy. Study quality was limited by spectrum bias, small samples, and scarce external validation, pre-analytic variation and batch effects were under-reported. Overall, salivary microbiological testing shows promising accuracy for screening and risk stratification of periodontitis and early childhood caries, but broader, multicenter validation and standardized workflows are required before routine clinical adoption.

title: Epigenetics approaches in Public Health for Cancer Prevention
description: Epigenetics and Public Health Cancer Prevention Author: Dr Siddalingaiah H. S. Professor of Community Medicine, Shridevi Institute of Medical Sciences & Research Hospital (SIMS & RH), Tumkur, Karnataka, India 📧 hssling@yahoo.com Running Title: Epigenetics and Public Health Cancer Prevention Abstract Background: Epigenetic mechanisms—DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNAs—mediate the effects of modifiable environmental and behavioural exposures on carcinogenesis. Because these molecular marks are reversible, they represent promising targets for population-level prevention. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, a systematic search (PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science; 2005–2025) identified human studies linking modifiable exposures or interventions with epigenetic endpoints relevant to cancer. Data were synthesised narratively and, for methylated SEPT9 (mSEPT9) colorectal-cancer screening, drawn from verified meta-analyses. Results: From 12 376 records, 324 human studies met inclusion. Environmental toxicants (arsenic, PM₂․₅, cadmium, pesticides) consistently produced gene-specific hyper- or hypomethylation associated with elevated cancer risk. Dietary and behavioural interventions—adequate folate and B-vitamins, polyphenol-rich foods, physical activity, and stress reduction—showed measurable correction of aberrant methylation. Meta-analysed mSEPT9 data yielded pooled sensitivity 0.78 (95 % CI 0.73–0.82) and specificity 0.84 (0.80–0.88). Conclusions: Epigenetic surveillance can enhance policy accountability for clean air, safe water, and balanced nutrition while enabling precision prevention and accessible, non-invasive screening. Keywords: Epigenetics; Cancer prevention; DNA methylation; Public health; Colorectal cancer screening; LMIC policy.   1. Introduction Cancer remains one of the foremost public-health challenges of the 21st century, responsible for an estimated 10 million deaths annually worldwide. Traditional prevention strategies—tobacco control, infection prevention, vaccination, and occupational-hazard reduction—have substantially lowered incidence for some sites, yet the global burden continues to rise as industrialisation, pollution, and ageing populations expand the pool of exposed individuals [1]. In this context, epigenetics —the study of heritable, reversible modifications in gene expression that occur without alteration of the DNA sequence—offers a powerful mechanistic framework to understand how social and environmental determinants translate into cancer risk [2, 3]. Epigenetic mechanisms and cancer development Epigenetic regulation occurs through three principal processes: (a) DNA methylation at cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) islands, which typically silences transcription; (b) post-translational histone modifications such as acetylation and methylation that remodel chromatin accessibility; and (c) non-coding RNAs (microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs) that fine-tune mRNA stability and translation [4]. In cancer, these mechanisms become dysregulated—tumour-suppressor genes are silenced (e.g. p16 , BRCA1 ), oncogenes are activated, and genomic instability increases [5]. Crucially, these aberrations can be triggered by exposures that are preventable or modifiable within a population framework. The public-health perspective Epigenetic research historically resided within molecular oncology, but growing evidence now links epigenetic marks to community-level exposures such as air pollution , arsenic in groundwater , pesticide residues , tobacco smoke , alcohol consumption , poor diet , and psychosocial stress [6–8]. Because epigenetic alterations are potentially reversible, they provide both biological indicators of exposure and targets for intervention . This dual property makes epigenetics particularly relevant to public health: it enables risk stratification, early detection, and evaluation of policy interventions. Rationale for LMIC-focused integration Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bear a disproportionate share of environmentally mediated cancers. India, for example, faces co-existing challenges of arsenic-contaminated groundwater in eastern states, indoor biomass-fuel smoke exposure among women, rapid urban air-pollution escalation, and nutrition transitions that produce both deficiencies and excesses [9]. Epigenetic epidemiology provides an opportunity to quantify the biological consequences of these social inequities and to design precision-public-health interventions that address them before clinical disease manifests. Policy convergence Epigenetic science aligns naturally with the Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3) commitment to reduce premature mortality from non-communicable diseases. It also complements India’s National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) and National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) , both of which now call for molecular-epidemiologic surveillance. Recognising epigenetic biomarkers as measurable intermediates between environment and disease can strengthen these programmes by enabling “mechanism-informed policy.” Objectives This review therefore aims to: 1.      Synthesize human evidence connecting modifiable exposures and epigenetic changes relevant to carcinogenesis. 2.      Identify public-health interventions—nutritional, behavioural, and environmental—that demonstrate epigenetic modulation. 3.      Summarise validated epigenetic biomarkers usable for population screening. 4.      Discuss translational implications for LMIC cancer-control policy and research capacity building.   2. Methods Study design and reporting A systematic review approach was adopted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines [10]. The protocol was designed in accordance with PROSPERO principles (registration pending). Both quantitative (meta-analytic) and qualitative syntheses were planned; however, de-novo pooling was limited to endpoints with existing harmonised data. Search strategy Electronic databases— PubMed , EMBASE , Scopus , and Web of Science —were searched for the period 1 January 2005 to 31 October 2025 using the following Boolean string: (“epigenetic” OR “DNA methylation” OR “histone modification” OR “microRNA” OR “epigenome”) AND (“cancer” OR “neoplas*”) AND (“prevention” OR “screening” OR “public health” OR “environmental exposure” OR “nutrition” OR “policy”). Grey literature was searched in WHO Global Health Library , NIEHS Environmental Epigenomics database , and IARC Monographs . Reference lists of major reviews were manually screened for additional eligible papers. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion: Human observational or interventional studies reporting at least one epigenetic endpoint (DNA methylation, histone modification, or miRNA) linked to a recognised cancer risk factor, preventive intervention, or early-detection biomarker. Studies reporting population or community-level exposures or interventions. Exclusion: In-vitro or animal studies without human validation. Clinical therapeutic trials using epigenetic drugs for established cancers unless discussing chemopreventive potential. Abstract-only conference proceedings and non-English texts lacking data tables. Screening and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts; full-text eligibility disagreements were resolved by consensus. Data were extracted on study design, setting, population, exposure/intervention, epigenetic marker, tissue source, outcome measure, and key findings. A PRISMA flow diagram (Fig 1) summarises the process: 12 376 records identified → 742 full texts assessed → 324 studies included. Quality assessment Observational studies: ROBINS-I domains (confounding, selection, measurement bias). Diagnostic biomarker studies: QUADAS-2 criteria (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing). Intervention trials: Cochrane RoB-2 for randomisation and outcome assessment. Studies were graded as low , moderate , or high risk of bias; only low/moderate were included in narrative synthesis. Data synthesis and analysis Given heterogeneous outcome metrics (percent methylation, β-value changes, miRNA fold-changes), a narrative and tabular synthesis was conducted for most domains. For colorectal-cancer blood tests based on methylated SEPT9 (mSEPT9), quantitative results were derived from existing peer-reviewed meta-analyses [11, 12]. Forest plots display pooled sensitivity 0.78 [95 % CI 0.73–0.82] and specificity 0.84 [0.80–0.88]. Where possible, 95 % confidence intervals were recalculated using the generic inverse-variance method in R (‘meta’ package). Policy-context extraction Beyond biomedical results, each eligible paper was coded for public-health relevance —defined as explicit discussion of exposure prevention, behavioural modification, screening, or policy translation. These data informed the “Implications for Policy and Practice” subsections of the Discussion. 3. Results 3.1 Overview of included studies The search identified 12 376 unique records , of which 324 human studies met eligibility criteria. These comprised: 126 observational cohort studies on environmental and occupational exposures; 128 nutritional or behavioural intervention studies; 50 biomarker validation and screening studies; and 20 mixed-design or life-course studies assessing early-life or transgenerational epigenetic effects. Most investigations originated from North America, Europe, and East Asia; a growing but smaller body emerged from India, Bangladesh, and China. Tissue sources varied: peripheral blood (58 %), buccal or saliva DNA (14 %), colon or breast tissue (12 %), and placenta or cord blood (6 %). Heterogeneity in assay methodology was substantial, yet patterns were remarkably consistent across regions and techniques when grouped by exposure category.   3.2 Environmental and occupational exposures 3.2.1 Inorganic arsenic Arsenic contamination of groundwater remains one of the most extensively documented environmental epigenetic hazards. Populations chronically exposed to concentrations > 50 µg/L show global hypomethylation and promoter hypermethylation of tumour-suppressor genes including p16INK4a , p53 , RASSF1A , and DAPK1 [13–15]. Studies from Bangladesh, Chile, and West Bengal demonstrated dose–response relationships between urinary arsenic and methylation levels, independent of nutritional status. Altered DNA methyltransferase (DNMT1) expression has been proposed as a mechanistic link. Public-health implication: Arsenic-induced methylation patterns support the rationale for universal groundwater testing and mitigation programmes such as well-switching and filtration in South Asia. Epigenetic monitoring of high-exposure districts can complement chemical surveillance by providing a biological early-warning system . 3.2.2 Air pollution (PM₂․₅ and diesel exhaust) Ambient particulate matter exposure induces LINE-1 and Alu hypomethylation , reflecting global genomic instability [16, 17]. Cohorts in Italy, China, and Mexico observed mean decreases of 0.8–1.5 % in LINE-1 methylation per 10 µg/m³ increase in PM₂․₅. Parallel up-regulation of inflammatory genes (IL-6, TNF-α) and hypermethylation of TP53 and MGMT have been reported [18]. Emerging studies link prenatal PM₂․₅ exposure to altered methylation of oxidative-stress genes in cord blood. Public-health implication: These findings justify stricter ambient-air-quality standards and household clean-fuel initiatives , reinforcing that air-pollution control is not merely respiratory protection but also cancer prevention through epigenetic stability . 3.2.3 Heavy metals and pesticides Cadmium and lead exposures alter GSTP1 and p16 methylation; organophosphate pesticides dysregulate miRNAs related to DNA repair [19]. Agricultural-worker studies in India and Egypt revealed cumulative changes correlating with duration of exposure. Policy translation: Integrating periodic biomonitoring of epigenetic markers in occupational-health schemes (Factories Act, 1948, India) could provide early detection of carcinogenic risk. Table 1. Randomised trials in China and the USA show that daily folate supplementation (400 µg) for 12 weeks increases global LINE-1 methylation by 1–3 % in peripheral blood of deficient adults [20]. Conversely, excessive folate in individuals with existing adenomas may promote proliferation, underscoring the need for life-stage-specific dosing [21]. 3.3.2 Phytochemicals and bioactive foods Polyphenols such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) from green tea, resveratrol from grapes, and curcumin from turmeric act as DNMT and HDAC inhibitors , reactivating silenced tumour-suppressor genes in pre-neoplastic cells [22]. Human supplementation trials in high-risk smokers demonstrated demethylation of p16 and MGMT promoters after 12 weeks of green-tea catechin intake [23]. 3.3.3 Physical activity and stress modulation Exercise modulates methylation of metabolic and inflammatory genes. The HERITAGE and CARDIA cohorts showed inverse associations between habitual physical activity and methylation of NRF2 and TNF-α promoters [24]. Stress-reduction interventions reduce cortisol-related methylation at NR3C1 , suggesting psychosocial routes to epigenetic resilience. Table 2. The 2-of-3 PCR algorithm yields higher specificity (0.96) at modest sensitivity reduction. Addition of mSDC2 or LINC00473 to mSEPT9 panels raises combined sensitivity to 0.85–0.88 [12]. Public-health interpretation: Although less sensitive than faecal-immunochemical testing (FIT), mSEPT9 is blood-based and thus valuable where stool-based screening has low acceptance. It could be offered through Ayushman Bharat Health & Wellness Centres for opportunistic screening of adults > 45 years who refuse colonoscopy. 3.4.2 Emerging biomarkers mSDC2: Sensitivity ≈ 0.81, specificity ≈ 0.90; effective for early lesions. miR-21, miR-92a: Detectable in plasma; elevated in adenomas and early CRC. Urinary 5-hmC signatures: Show promise for bladder-cancer risk in smokers. Figure 2. Forest plot of pooled sensitivity and specificity for plasma mSEPT9. (Insert forest plot; pooled diagnostic odds ratio ≈ 18.6 [95 % CI 14–25]).   3.5 Early-life and transgenerational epigenetic effects Studies from the Mother–Child Arsenic and Air-Pollution cohorts demonstrate that in-utero exposures can imprint the foetal epigenome. Altered methylation of genes governing immune response ( IL-8 , IFN-γ ) and metabolism ( LEP , IGF2 ) has been observed in cord blood, persisting into childhood [25, 26]. Animal-to-human translational evidence suggests some marks may transmit across generations via germline epimutations. Policy significance: Protecting pregnant women from environmental and nutritional stressors can prevent intergenerational amplification of cancer risk —an ethical and economic imperative for LMICs. Integrating maternal-exposure surveillance into reproductive and child-health programmes (e.g., Anemia-Mukt Bharat, POSHAN 2.0) could yield long-term cancer-prevention dividends. 3.6 PRISMA flow summary Figure 1.
